prompts.title: The Universal Locator
prompts.prompt:
Below is a document and a question about it. Answer the question using only this document, and make every claim carry the line it rests on.

For each claim in your answer, give me three things in this order:

CLAIM: what you are asserting, in one sentence.
QUOTE: the exact sentence from the document that the claim rests on, verbatim, inside quote marks. Where a claim rests on more than one sentence, quote all of them, separately. Do not join them with an ellipsis.
WHERE: the section number or heading the quoted sentence sits under, and the page where the document shows one.

If you cannot find a line that carries a claim, write NOT FOUND against it and move on. NOT FOUND is a correct answer here and I would rather have it than a sentence that sits near the point.

---
NOT FOUND means you could not find a line, not that the document is silent. Word it that way every time.
Do not paraphrase inside the quote marks. A tidied quote is a summary of one sentence, and it cannot be searched for, which is the only reason the quote is there at all.
Do not fill a gap with what the document probably means, what a document of this type usually says, or anything you know from outside it.
Do not rank your claims, do not tell me which one matters most, and do not close with an overall assessment.

The question:
[state it in one sentence]

The document:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Make every claim carry the verbatim line it rests on, and make NOT FOUND a permitted answer.

prompts.title: Sort It Into Three Lists
prompts.prompt:
Here is an answer you produced about a document, and the document itself. Do not defend the answer and do not improve it. Sort it.

Take every claim in the answer and put it in exactly one of three lists:

DIRECTLY STATED: a line in the document says this. Quote the line, verbatim, with its section.
INFERRED: no single line says it. You concluded it from what is there. Name the two or three lines you built it from, quoted, and say in one line what the step between them was.
NOT FOUND: you cannot support it from this document at all.

Close with one line: how many claims landed in each list.

---
Every claim goes somewhere. A claim you cannot place is a NOT FOUND, not a DIRECTLY STATED with a loose quote attached to it.
INFERRED is not a confession and I am not asking you to withdraw those claims. I am asking to know which parts of my answer are a reading rather than a quote, because a reading is where somebody sensible could have read it differently.
Do not move a claim into DIRECTLY STATED on the strength of a line that mentions the subject. The line has to carry the claim.
Do not add claims that were not in the answer, and do not merge two claims into one to make them easier to place.

The answer:
[paste]

The document:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Split an answer into what the document states, what was inferred from it, and what cannot be supported at all.

prompts.title: Does The Quote Carry The Claim
prompts.prompt:
Here is a set of claims, each with a quoted line and a section reference, and the document they came from. I am not asking whether the claims are true. I am asking one question of each pair, and only that question: does the quoted line carry the claim, or does it merely sit near it?

Sort every pair into four buckets:

CARRIES IT: the quoted line settles the claim on its own.
NARROWER: the line supports a smaller version of the claim. State the smaller version in one sentence.
ADJACENT: the line is about the same subject and settles nothing. Say what it does settle.
NOT IN THE DOCUMENT: the quoted line does not appear in the document in that form. Give the nearest thing you can find, or write no near match.

For every pair that is not CARRIES IT, add one line: what a line that did carry the claim would have to say.

---
This is the failure the whole exercise exists for, so treat ADJACENT as the default and make each pair earn CARRIES IT.
Check the quote against the document word by word before you accept it. A citation to a real section that does not support the claim is more expensive than no citation at all, because it arrives with a verification handle attached and spends the doubt I would otherwise have kept.
Where the quoted line depends on a definition or an exception elsewhere in the document, quote that too. A line that carries a claim only until you read the carve-out is NARROWER, not CARRIES IT.
Do not re-answer the original question, and do not offer me better claims.

The claims and their citations:
[paste]

The document:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Catch the expensive failure: a real citation to a real section that does not actually support the claim.

prompts.title: The Universal Document Map
prompts.prompt:
Below is a document. Do not summarise it and do not answer any question about it yet. Map it.

Work through it in the order it is written, and for every section give me exactly three things:

HEADING: the heading exactly as it appears, including its number. Where a block has no heading, write NO HEADING and give its first six words instead.
DOES: what that section does, in one line. Pick the verb: defines, obliges, limits, prices, grants, prohibits, describes a process, assigns responsibility, states an exception, or provides background only.
CONTAINS: whether the section holds a number, a date, a named obligation, or an exception. Say which of the four, or write none.

Then two lists, and these are the point of the exercise:

MISMATCHES: any section whose heading does not match what is actually inside it.
ORPHANS: anything substantial sitting under no heading at all. Quote its first line.

---
DOES is one line and it is a job title, not a precis. "Defines what counts as personal data" is right. "Discusses the definition of personal data and explains how it applies throughout" is a summary wearing a costume. Where you cannot name what a section does in one line, write UNCLEAR and move on.
Do not rank sections by importance, do not tell me what matters, and do not give an overall assessment. Do not answer the question I am obviously going to ask next.
Where you cannot see something, write not present in what I can see. Never state that the document does not contain something.

The document:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Make a long document hand back its own shape before you ask it a single question.

prompts.title: Aim Before You Fire
prompts.prompt:
Here is a map of a document, and the decision I actually have to make. Sort the map against the decision. Do not answer anything yet.

BEARS ON IT: the sections that could change the decision. For each one: the single question I should put to that section, and what a BAD answer to that question would look like, so I can recognise one when it arrives.
DOES NOT: the sections that cannot change the decision, with the reason in a few words.
CANNOT TELL: any section where the map does not carry enough for you to place it. Say what you would need to know.

---
The bad-answer line is not optional and it is not a warning about invented facts. It is the shape of an answer that sounds responsive and does not settle the question: an answer that restates the section back to me, an answer that gives me a principle where I need a number, an answer that covers the general case when I asked about the exception.
Do not answer any of the questions you generate. Do not recommend a decision. Do not tell me the document broadly supports or does not support anything.

The map:
[paste the output of The Universal Document Map]

The decision I have to make:
[state it in one sentence, including the option you are leaning towards]
prompts.use_case: Turn a map into the short list of sections that can actually change your decision, and the question to put to each.

prompts.title: Check The Map Against The Contents
prompts.prompt:
Here are two things: a map you produced of a document, and that document's own contents page. Diff them against each other and report only the differences.

IN THE CONTENTS, NOT IN THE MAP: every section the contents page lists that does not appear in the map. Give the heading and number exactly as the contents page has them. This list is the finding.
IN THE MAP, NOT IN THE CONTENTS: every section the map has that the contents page does not list. Unlisted sections are worth as much as skipped ones.
SAME SECTION, DIFFERENT HEADING: where both have it but the wording differs, show both wordings side by side.
NUMBERING BREAKS: any gap, repeat or out-of-order number in either one.

---
Report the differences and stop. Do not rebuild the map, do not explain a gap away, and do not tell me a difference is probably just formatting. A section that is in the contents and not in the map is exactly the section I would never have known to ask about.
Where the two agree completely, say so in one line rather than padding the output.

The map:
[paste]

The contents page or section list, copied from the document:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Diff a map against the document's own contents page, because the sections it skipped are the ones you would never think to ask about.

prompts.title: Grade The Draft Against The Brief
prompts.prompt:
Below are two things: the brief I gave, and the draft that came back. Grade the draft against the brief, line by line. Do not fix anything and do not rewrite anything.

Break my brief into its individual requirements first, one per line, including the ones I stated as constraints or format rather than content. Then mark every requirement:

MET, and quote the words in the draft that meet it
MISSED, and quote the words in the draft that fall short, plus what the brief asked for instead
IGNORED, meaning nothing in the draft attempts it at all

Then rank every MISSED and IGNORED by what it costs the person who reads this draft, worst first. Cost means what that reader does wrong, misunderstands, or fails to do because of it. Say the cost out loud for each one.

---
A MISSED you cannot support with a quote from the draft is not a MISSED. Delete it. Do not grade tone, elegance or flow unless my brief asked for them. Do not tell me the draft is strong overall, does a good job, or captures the essence of anything. Do not offer a single word of replacement text. The output is a graded list and nothing else.

My brief:
[paste the original instructions you gave]

The draft:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Make the model grade its own draft against your brief, quoted and ranked, before you touch anything.

prompts.title: Split Defects From Taste
prompts.prompt:
Here is a brief and the draft that came back. I have opinions about this draft and I cannot tell which of them matter. Sort my problem with it into two lists and nothing else.

BREAKS THE BRIEF: things that fail a requirement I actually stated. For each one, quote the requirement, quote the line in the draft, and say in one sentence what breaks.

JUST DIFFERENT: things that are a legitimate choice the writer made, which I might not have made, but which no requirement rules out. For each one, quote the line and name the preference it collides with, whether that preference is mine or a convention.

Put every item in exactly one list. Where something sits on the line, put it in JUST DIFFERENT and say what I would have to add to my brief to move it across.

---
Do not fix anything from either list. Do not tell me which JUST DIFFERENT items you would change anyway. Length, structure, word choice and register all belong in JUST DIFFERENT unless my brief set them. If BREAKS THE BRIEF comes back empty, say so plainly rather than promoting something to fill it.

My brief:
[paste the original instructions you gave]

The draft:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Separate what actually fails your brief from what is simply not how you would have written it.

prompts.title: Rank The Misses By Reader Cost
prompts.prompt:
Here is a draft and a list of things wrong with it. The list is longer than the round I have time for. Order it by what each miss costs the person who reads this, and draw a line under what is worth fixing now.

For each item on my list, one line each:
- The reader consequence: what that person does wrong, misunderstands, or fails to do because of it. Where you cannot name a consequence, write NO READER COST
- Who pays it: the decision maker, someone downstream of them, or only me

Then output the list in a single order, worst consequence first, and put a line labelled CUT HERE at the point where the remaining items stop changing what the reader does. Everything below that line stays in the draft this round.

Finish with any reader cost you can see in the draft that is not on my list at all, marked NOT ON YOUR LIST.

---
Rank by consequence, not by how easy the fix looks and not by how wrong it feels to me. Where two items carry the same consequence, give them the same rank and say so rather than inventing a tiebreak. Do not fix anything above or below the line. Do not tell me the whole list is worth doing anyway.

The draft:
[paste]

My list of what is wrong with it:
[paste, one per line]
prompts.use_case: Turn a long list of complaints into an ordered fix list with a cut line drawn under it.

prompts.title: Status Update Cold Read
prompts.prompt:
Someone forwarded me this status update with no message of their own on it. I do not know the project, the author, or what any earlier update said. You are [the reader, e.g. a steering committee sponsor who funds this and sees it once a month]. Read it once, at the speed that person would read it, caring about what they care about, and tell me what you came away believing.

Report back:
- Your one line verdict on how the work is going, in your own words
- Whether it reads as getting better, getting worse, or as a flat snapshot with no direction in it. Quote the words that put you there, and if there are none, say the update gave you no sense of direction at all
- Anything you took as off track, and the line that put it there. For each one, say whether the update calls it off track or you concluded that yourself
- Who you think is holding the work right now, and whether anyone is waiting on anyone
- What you believe happens next, and by when
- The first thing you would have to go and ask before you could act on any of it

---
Answer only from what is written. Do not guess at what the writer meant or at anything that happened outside the update. If something is not on the page, say it is not on the page. Keep off the writing itself.

Status update:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Find out what a stakeholder actually believes about project health after reading your update.

prompts.title: Project Brief Reverse Brief
prompts.prompt:
I found this project brief in a shared folder with no covering note and no author on it. I am telling you nothing else about it. Work backwards from the page alone and reconstruct the instructions you think the writer was given before they sat down to write it.

Reconstruct, in this order:
- The objective this brief exists to serve, in one sentence
- The audience it was written for, and how you can tell
- The one decision or action it wants from that audience
- The constraints the writer was clearly told about: money, dates, scope, people, anything fixed
- What success looks like, and how anyone would know it had been reached
- Anything the writer appears to have been told not to do: a boundary, an exclusion, an option ruled out before they started. Quote the words that carry it

For each item, quote the words on the page that let you recover it. Where the page does not carry an item, mark it NOT RECOVERABLE and move on. Do not close the gap with a sensible guess.

---
Everything you say has to trace back to a line in the brief. Do not tell me what the writer probably intended. Do not write a better brief and do not offer wording changes. A short list with several NOT RECOVERABLE entries is the right answer if that is what the page supports.

Project brief:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Recover the objective, audience and ask a brief carries, and see what it never carried at all.

prompts.title: Escalation Email Cold Read
prompts.prompt:
This email arrived in my inbox first thing this morning. You are [the reader, e.g. the ops manager it is addressed to, who owns the rota but not the budget]. I have never met the sender and I know nothing about the situation it describes. Read it as that person and tell me what landed.

Tell me:
- What you think the sender wants from you specifically, in one sentence
- The deadline you think you are working to, and whether the email states it or you filled it in
- Who you think owns the next move: you, the sender, or someone else named in the email
- What you would actually do with it: stop what you are doing and handle it now, fit it in before the end of today, put it somewhere this week, or leave it sitting. Pick one and quote the exact words that put it there
- Anything you would have to go and ask before you could do what it wants

---
I want what reached you, not what the sender was trying to achieve. Where the ask or the deadline is not spelled out, say it is missing rather than supplying the one that would make sense. No redraft, and no notes on how it is written.

Email:
[paste]
prompts.use_case: Check whether the reader of an escalation knows what you want from them and how soon.
